summary: The fourth DVDASA episode begins immediately after Episode Three and first turns Bobby Namba's need to leave—his girlfriend Carol is waiting—into an argument about work, friendship, obligation, and the silent treatment. Before he goes, the group discusses travel and the Hong Kong club in Tijuana, then plays a Michael J. Fox trivia round. With Bobby gone, the remaining conversation repeatedly tries and fails to become wholesome: sexual-health practices lead into language and consent, Yoshi's escalating moral hypotheticals, Asa's account of being assaulted at a concert, debates about reporting and marital consent, embarrassment on Japanese trains, and three overlapping arrest and jail stories. The episode is most useful as evidence of the show's format: serious experiences and ethical disagreements are continually pulled into provocation, competition, and autobiographical performance.

connections.label: The show itself becomes a relationship obligation
connections.note: Bobby enjoys the recording and also treats leaving on time as part of caring for Carol. David frames participation as friendship and paid work. The conflict exposes how the podcast turns informal intimacy into a recurring production demand.

connections.label: Wholesome structure repeatedly collapses
connections.note: Bobby's trivia is intended to bring the room from darkness into light. After he leaves, each attempt to stabilize the tone moves back toward explicit health, assault, coercion, jail, or humiliation. The failure is a reliable formal feature, not just a topic list.

connections.label: Consent appears in incompatible frames
connections.note: The episode moves among transactional negotiation, an assault by a stranger, whether to report it, marital expectations, and an imagined sexual contract. These should remain separate cases; the participants' attempt to collapse them into one argument is itself the editorial finding.

connections.label: Crime stories are also class stories
connections.note: Asa describes entitlement and adolescent shoplifting, while David links organized food theft during art school to crowded housing, expensive books, and hunger. Neither context erases the act, but the motives and retrospective meanings differ.

connections.label: Humiliation becomes performed evidence
connections.note: The Japanese-train story and all three jail accounts turn private embarrassment into comic proof of character. The telling makes shame useful to the show while preserving the speaker's claim that the original experience was frightening or degrading.

quality.speaker_state: four recurring participants; Bobby exits early; named turns withheld
quality.content_note: The episode contains explicit sexual material, offensive language, hypothetical harm involving children and illness, discussion of assault and marital rape, crime, incarceration, and racial harassment. Editorial structure does not endorse the participants' claims.
